about: Third-party models used as visual stand-ins for structures that are not pyramids. None is a measurement: each is placed on the OSM footprint of what it stands for (centroid, principal axis and length along it), and nothing about its form is entered in data/. `python scripts/models.py` downloads them into build/models/ (gitignored) through the Sketchfab API with the token in SKETCHFAB_TOKEN or ~/.seked/keys.env; `blender/render_standins.py` fits them at render time and labels every one a stand-in.

models.name: The Great Sphinx of Giza
models.author: The Watt Institution
models.attribution: "The Great Sphinx of Giza" by The Watt Institution (https://sketchfab.com/wattinstitution), CC BY 4.0: a scan of Bert W. Longworth's cast bronze topographic model of the Sphinx, cast by François Rudier, exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1903. Cut from its plinth, decimated and refitted.
models.why: A sculptor's topographic model of 1903 rather than a survey, and of the Sphinx as it stood then, sand to its chest: its forepaws and the lower body are under the sculpted sand, which Baraize did not clear until 1925 to 1936. So the proportions are an artist's and the pose is a century out of date. It is still far nearer the Sphinx than the three prisms OSM models it as, and it should be replaced when a scan of the excavated Sphinx can be had. Its bronze texture is dropped for the scene's own core limestone.
models.retired: 2026-09-16: replaced by sphinx-meshy, which stands free of the sand as the Sphinx does now. Kept so the render of snapshot 0019 can be remade.

models.name: The Great Sphinx of Giza, excavated
models.author: generated with Meshy from photographs
models.license: generated (Meshy paid plan: the output belongs to the account holder); photographs CC0
models.attribution: Generated by Meshy (multi-image to 3D) from four CC0 photographs on Wikimedia Commons: "Sphinx with the third pyramid.jpg" and three of "The Great Sphinx, Giza, GG, EGY" (40936134053, 47113253734, 47850555412). Not a scan: an image model's reconstruction of the excavated Sphinx, cut, decimated and refitted to the OSM outline.
models.why: The Watt model is the Sphinx of 1903, buried to the chest. This one is generated from photographs taken since the enclosure was cleared, so the paws, the rump and the tail stand free as they do now. Its form is a model's guess from four views, not a survey. It came back as one connected piece that includes the scaffolding standing against the chest and rump in three of the photographs, which is left on (the Sphinx is rarely without some); a loose block beside it is dropped. Its long axis is taken as its own front (-y), because the scaffolding turned its principal axis 6 degrees off. Fitted by length it stands 24 m against OSM's 21: the generated rump is short for its height, and the length is kept as the fit because the footprint is what is known.

models.author: generated with Meshy from photographs, restored by its image model
models.name: The Great Sphinx of Giza, as carved
models.license: generated (Meshy paid plan: the output belongs to the account holder); photographs CC0
models.attribution: Generated by Meshy: four CC0 photographs of the Sphinx on Wikimedia Commons, restored by its image-to-image model to the Sphinx as finished, then built into a mesh by multi-image to 3D. A reconstruction, not a scan: the body's proportions come from the photographs, and the nose, uraeus, beard, dressed stone and paint only from the prompt.
models.why: For --state built. The Sphinx as it was finished, with the parts it has since lost: the nose, the uraeus on the brow, the plaited beard whose fragments are in the British Museum and Cairo, the striped nemes, the red of the face whose traces survive. Nothing of its form is measured; its length is the outline's.

meshy.image_prompt: Edit this photograph of the Great Sphinx of Giza to show it newly finished in the Fourth Dynasty, about 2500 BC. Keep the camera position, the framing, and the Sphinx's body, pose and proportions exactly as they are. Restore only what has been lost: an intact nose, a rearing cobra uraeus on the brow, a long plaited divine beard under the chin, the nemes headdress crisply carved, and every surface smoothly dressed in fresh pale limestone with no erosion, no cracks and no repair blocks. Paint it as the Egyptians did, in matt earth pigments: red ochre on the face, the nemes striped in muted yellow ochre and blue, no gold and no gloss. Remove all scaffolding, fences, tourists and modern buildings; the ground around it is clean, level pale stone.

models.author: generated with Meshy from photographs, changed by its image model
models.name: The Sphinx as a lion (hypothesis)
models.license: generated (Meshy paid plan: the output belongs to the account holder); photographs CC0
models.attribution: Generated by Meshy: four CC0 photographs of the Sphinx on Wikimedia Commons, first restored by its image-to-image model as a recumbent Anubis, then given a lion's head in the same pose, then built into a mesh by multi-image to 3D. It illustrates a claim, that the Sphinx was first carved as a lion and its head later recut (Hancock and Bauval 1996 among others); no lion head survives, so nothing of this form is evidence.
models.why: Shown only with --sphinx lion in today's state: the lion's head on the Sphinx's body, weathered as the body is now. The freshly carved lion of the ancient and built states is sphinx-lion-fresh.

meshy.image_prompt: This image shows a colossal recumbent statue carved from layered honey-coloured limestone, with a jackal's head. Change only the head: replace the jackal's head with a lion's head carved in the same stone, in the same position and turned exactly the same way as the jackal's head is turned in this image, so the lion looks where the jackal looks. The lion's head is stylised in the manner of ancient Egyptian stone lion statues: a broad, calm, heavy-browed face with a short muzzle and small rounded ears, and the mane carved as a smooth ruff with shallow grooves that falls onto the chest in two broad lappets like a nemes headdress; no fur texture, no flowing hair, not a photograph of a real lion and not a European lion. It is in proportion to the massive body and cut from the same weathered outcrop, so head and body read as one sculpture. Keep everything else in the image exactly as it is.

meshy.image_prompt: This image shows a colossal recumbent statue of a lion carved from honey-coloured limestone, with a stylised Egyptian lion's head and a mane falling in lappets like a nemes headdress. Show the same statue on the day it was finished, freshly carved: keep the camera, the framing, the pose, the lion's head and the direction it faces, the lappets, the long forepaws and every proportion exactly as they are, but make every surface smoothly dressed and finished, with crisp clean edges and fine chisel-smoothed stone. Remove all erosion, weathering, deep horizontal gullies, cracks, crumbling, missing chunks and repair blocks; the body is a clean continuous sculpted form of a lying lion, with its haunches, flanks and legs modelled, not a worn rock. Keep the same warm limestone colour. Remove all scaffolding, loose blocks, fences, tourists and modern buildings.

models.license: generated (Meshy paid plan: the output belongs to the account holder); photographs CC0
models.attribution: Generated by Meshy: four CC0 photographs of the Sphinx on Wikimedia Commons, given a jackal's head by its image-to-image model, then built into a mesh by multi-image to 3D. It illustrates a claim, Robert Temple's in The Sphinx Mystery (2009), that the monument was first a recumbent Anubis whose head was later recut; no such head survives, so nothing of this form is evidence.
models.why: Shown only with --sphinx anubis in today's state: Robert Temple's recumbent Anubis on the Sphinx's body, weathered as the body is now. The freshly carved Anubis of the ancient and built states is sphinx-anubis-fresh.

meshy.image_prompt: Edit this photograph of the Great Sphinx of Giza to show it as if it had been carved from the start as a colossal recumbent Anubis, the jackal god. Keep the camera position, the framing, and the long recumbent body, the forepaws, the haunches and all proportions exactly as they are. Replace only the human face and head with a jackal's head in the style of Egyptian Anubis statues: a long narrow muzzle pointing straight ahead and tall upright pointed ears, the neck and chest carved as part of the rock. The head is carved from the same horizontally layered, honey-coloured limestone as the body, in the same weathered texture and colour, so it reads as one ancient sculpture cut from one outcrop. Remove all scaffolding, loose blocks, repair masonry, fences, tourists and modern buildings.

meshy.image_prompt: This image shows a colossal recumbent statue of the jackal god Anubis carved from honey-coloured limestone. Show the same statue on the day it was finished, freshly carved: keep the camera, the framing, the pose, the jackal head, the tall ears, the headdress lappets, the long forepaws and every proportion exactly as they are, but make every surface smoothly dressed and finished, with crisp clean edges and fine chisel-smoothed stone. Remove all erosion, weathering, deep horizontal gullies, cracks, crumbling, missing chunks and repair blocks; the body is a clean continuous sculpted form of a lying jackal, with its haunches, ribs and legs modelled, not a worn rock. Keep the same warm limestone colour. Remove all scaffolding, loose blocks, fences, tourists and modern buildings.

retexture.text_style_prompt: Ancient Egyptian monumental sculpture newly finished in honey-toned Giza limestone, photographed in desert sun: realistic stone texture with grain, pitting and subtle colour variation, sharp chisel-cut edges, deep shadows in carved grooves, faint tool marks on the broad planes of the body, the headdress pleats and ear edges picked out by slightly darker stone. Natural, unpainted, freshly quarried stone, no weathering damage.

retexture_tries.retex2: Freshly carved colossal statue in warm golden-cream limestone with a clearly visible natural stone grain: fine speckles, tiny fossil flecks and pores, soft mottled tonal variation from pale cream to light honey, and faint horizontal bedding lines running through the rock. Every carved detail is crisp and deeply cut with slightly darker recesses: the pleats of the headdress, the eyes, the collar, the ribs, the toes. Dressed matte stone, not painted, not plastic, no erosion, no cracks, no dirt.
retexture_tries.retex3: Ancient Egyptian monumental sculpture newly finished in honey-toned Giza limestone, photographed in desert sun: realistic stone texture with grain, pitting and subtle colour variation, sharp chisel-cut edges, deep shadows in carved grooves, faint tool marks on the broad planes of the body, the headdress pleats and ear edges picked out by slightly darker stone. Natural, unpainted, freshly quarried stone, no weathering damage.
retexture_tries.paint-black: Colossal ancient Egyptian statue of the jackal god Anubis on the day it was finished, carved in limestone and painted in rich matt mineral pigments: the whole jackal, head, body, legs and tail, painted deep glossy black like the Nile's fertile silt; the headdress lappets painted in bands of gold and deep lapis blue; a broad collar necklace on the chest in gold, turquoise, lapis blue and carnelian red beads; the eyes and inner ears outlined in gold; a gold band on the tail. Crisp carved detail, fine stone grain visible under the paint on the broad surfaces. No weathering, no cracks.
retexture_tries.paint-head: Colossal ancient Egyptian statue of the jackal god Anubis on the day it was finished: the body, legs and tail left as fine honey-coloured dressed limestone with visible stone grain, while the jackal head and neck are painted matt black with the eyes lined in gold and kohl, the headdress lappets painted in alternating gold and lapis blue stripes, and a broad painted collar on the chest in gold, turquoise and carnelian red bands. Crisp carved detail, no weathering, no cracks.
retexture_tries.paint-pale: Colossal ancient Egyptian statue of the jackal god Anubis on the day it was finished, carved in pale limestone with visible grain and painted in the restrained Old Kingdom manner: the jackal's face in dark charcoal black with a red ochre tongue line and eyes outlined in black and white, the headdress lappets striped in muted yellow ochre and faded blue, a broad collar in red ochre, blue and yellow bands, the body left in natural limestone with a faint warm wash. Matt pigments, crisp carved detail, no weathering.
retexture_tries.paint-black2: Colossal ancient Egyptian statue of the jackal god Anubis on the day it was finished, carved from limestone and painted: the whole jackal in deep matt charcoal-black mineral paint with a soft stone texture showing through, not glossy and not ceramic; the headdress lappets striped in real gold leaf and deep lapis-lazuli blue; a broad collar of gold, turquoise and carnelian bands on the chest; the eyes inlaid white and black and outlined in gold; thin gold bands on the ears' edges and the tail. Rich but restrained, like a royal temple statue. Crisp carved detail, no weathering.
retexture_tries.paint-pale2: Colossal ancient Egyptian statue of the jackal god Anubis on the day it was finished, carved in warm pale limestone with visible grain and painted in matt earth pigments: the jackal's head and neck in soft charcoal black, the eyes outlined in black with white, the headdress lappets striped in yellow ochre and Egyptian blue, a broad collar in red ochre, Egyptian blue and yellow ochre bands, a thin red ochre line on the tail; the body left in natural limestone. Matt, slightly chalky pigments, crisp carved detail, no weathering.

paint-black2.why: Chosen by Stewart on 2026-09-17 for the ancient state: the whole jackal in matt black paint, with gold leaf and lapis on the lappets and collar. Anubis is black in Egyptian painting and statuary; that this colossus was painted so is part of the claim, not evidence.

reconstructions.name: Giza Plateau by L.VII.C
reconstructions.author: gwenajello (Sketchfab), after L.VII.C on the 3D Warehouse
reconstructions.attribution: "Giza Plateau by L.VII.C" by gwenajello on Sketchfab, credited to L.VII.C on the SketchUp 3D Warehouse: a reconstruction of the plateau as built, registered onto the survey through its three pyramids, which are dropped for the database's.
reconstructions.why: The as-built state wants the complexes whole, and this model has them: the temples roofed, the causeways covered, the enclosure walls, the harbour basins and the cased queens' pyramids and mastabas, laid out after the Egyptological plans. Registered by its pyramids it lands within a few metres of the survey. Its forms are a reconstructor's; its Sphinx is dropped while a Sphinx stand-in is shown.
